newsitem.headline: AMLC Beef Weekly - Australian export prices.

AMLC COMMENTARY: Last Friday the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA) released the 1 July U.S. cattle inventory report. The report showed that U.S. cattle numbers were down in almost every category including:
- all cattle and calves 108.8 million head, down two percent on 1996 and four percent on 1995 and
- beef cows 34.7 million head, down three percent from 1996 and four percent from 1995.

The figures hold a number of important implications. Breeding stock numbers are down because of liquidation through 1995 and 1996. This reduction in cow inventories has led to a smaller calf crop. This calf crop represents the pool of slaughter cattle for 1998 and 1999.

Although liquidation has eased in the U.S. this year, there are still many heifers in feedlots which means the producers have not been replacing this year's cull cows. As beef cow operators become financially stronger (assisted by feeder cattle prices which are 50 percent above last year), they will begin to retain heifers for breeding.

This will mean a further reduction in available feeder cattle supplies, another tightening in feeder cattle prices (encouraging the retention of greater numbers of heifers), fewer heifers in the slaughter mix and lower production.

U.S. steer numbers are also well down. This will reduce the number of steers available for slaughter over the next two to three years. However, the decline in feed costs witnessed this year will allow feedlotters to offset, somewhat, the increased cost of feeder steers by increasing carcase weights. Carcase weights should rise towards the end of this year into 1998.
The U.S. cattle on feed report, also released last Friday, gives an indication that U.S. feedlotters are already beginning to think in this fashion.
Numbers on feed as at July 1 were 17 percent above last year (when numbers were sharply reduced because of escalating feed grain prices), but around one percent below 1995.
On international beef markets this week prices improved. The U.S. lean beef market rose by 10-19 Ac/kg for most manufacturing grades, prompted by a tightening in supplies.
Glancing at 90CL boneless beef contracts in early 1998, the February 1998 contract traded to 110USc/lb this week, a 10 percent premium to current cash market prices.
In Japan, although price movements varied across different products, assisted by a further weakening of the A$ against the yen, prices mostly improved by 1-4Ac/kg.

Australian exporters were extremely successful in the latest Korean tender awarded Tuesday, July 22. Local packers scored all the grassfed fullsets (684 tonnes) and grainfed quarter beef (400 tonnes) and the largest majority of the grassfed quarter component (3790 tonnes out of 4000 tonnes).

Back home, in livestock markets, prices were suppressed by unusually large winter offerings. Saleyard offerings, at 25,000 head, were extremely high in New South Wales (highest winter yarding on record) as dry conditions strengthened their hold on the state.
Cows and heifers, which are making up an increasingly larger proportion of yardings, traded on a generally easier trend.
Prices held firm for quality steers and bullocks which were in the minority at most sale centres.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
